tags.name: TripService
tags.description:
TripService owns the trip lifecycle and is the only writer of trip state.

Synchronous on purpose, and the contrast with the rest of the system is the
point. Location and matching are event-driven because they are streams: a
position is one of thousands a second and nobody waits for it. A rider
pressing "request ride" is waiting, and wants an answer — a fare, a trip id,
or a reason it cannot happen. Modelling that as an event and correlating a
reply would be an RPC with extra steps and worse error handling.
The HTTP mapping lives here, next to the RPC it maps, and grpc-gateway
generates the REST surface from it. That is the point: hand-written handlers
mean the REST API and the gRPC contract are two sources of truth, and the
first thing they do is drift — the reference this project borrows from has a
TypeScript contract file and a Go one that already disagree about which
events exist.

Paths follow Google's API design guide: plural collections, and custom
methods as `:verb` rather than as invented sub-resources.
## How the TypeScript client is named and typed from here

`packages/domain/src/api/SurgeApi.ts` is generated from the OpenAPI document
this file produces, so everything about the client's shape is decided here
rather than restated there:

- `tags` becomes the client group and `operation_id` the method, which is why
  they are `trips` and `create` rather than the defaults that would give
  `api.TripService.TripServiceCreateTrip(...)`.
- `format` carries the semantic type of a string. OpenAPI leaves `format` open
  deliberately, and it is the only annotation that survives the whole chain —
  proto, document, generated schema — including on path parameters. A field
  marked `trip-id` becomes a branded `TripId` in TypeScript; `int64`, which
  grpc-gateway sets on its own, becomes a decoded number rather than the
  quoted string proto3 puts on the wire.
- Every response declares `default` explicitly, because the gateway's error
  handler is custom and the generator's assumption would be wrong.

tags.name: DriverService
tags.description:
DriverService owns driver profiles and vehicles — the slow-moving facts.

Deliberately NOT where driver location lives. Positions arrive ten thousand
times a second and are answered from the matcher's in-memory index; putting
them behind an RPC would be a synchronous call per ping, which is the thing
this whole architecture exists to avoid.

tags.name: SimulatorService
tags.description:
SimulatorService is the load generator's control panel: how many drivers,
reporting how often.

Behind the gateway like every other API, rather than on the simulator's own
port, for two reasons. The console should reach one origin with one token.
And turning the knob from 500 drivers to 50,000 is an operation on shared
infrastructure, so it is ops only — enforced by the simulator itself against
the caller the gateway forwards, the same way the trip service enforces who
may read a trip.

tags.name: PaymentsService
tags.description:
PaymentsService is what riders and drivers see of money.

Reads of what the payments service has stored, and the two moments a person
has to hand something over to the processor: a rider's card, and a driver's
identity for payouts. Neither ever passes through here. A card is typed into
the processor's own form in the browser, which this only starts; a driver's
details go to the processor's hosted onboarding, which this only links to.

Nothing that moves money is an endpoint. Holds, captures and transfers
happen because a trip was requested or completed, not because a client
asked — a client that could ask could ask twice.

The caller is never a field, as in trip.proto: it arrives as metadata from
the gateway's verified token.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description:
Page size. Clamped by the server; a client asking for everything gets a
page, because "return the whole table" is not a request a public API
should honour.

parameters.name: pageToken
parameters.description:
Opaque cursor from a previous response. Opaque on purpose: a client that
decodes it is a client that breaks when the ordering changes.

post.summary:
ArriveTrip, StartTrip and CompleteTrip are the driver's half of the
lifecycle: accepted → arrived → in progress → completed.
post.description:
Only the driver the trip is assigned to may call them, and the trip service
enforces that rather than the gateway, for the same reason ownership is
enforced there on reads: only the service knows whose trip it is. A caller
who is not the assigned driver gets NotFound, because confirming a trip
exists to someone who may not touch it is itself a disclosure.

No body: the trip id in the path is the whole request, and the caller is
metadata like everywhere else.
Arrive: the driver is at the pickup.

default.description: The gateway's error shape, from its custom error handler.

post.summary: Cancel ends a trip before completion.
post.description:
A custom method rather than DELETE: cancelling is a state transition that
returns the trip, not a deletion — the row stays, and a rider can still
read what happened to it.

default.description: The gateway's error shape, from its custom error handler.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description:
The caller is NOT a field on any request.

It arrives as gRPC metadata, put there by the gateway from a verified token.
This matters more now that the REST body maps straight onto the message: a
`rider_id` field would be client-supplied, and a client that can name the
rider can quote, book and read rides as somebody else.

availableCents.description: In the driver's balance and free to withdraw.

pendingCents.description: In the driver's balance and not yet settled.

owedCents.description: Earned and not yet sent to their balance: waiting on onboarding.

v1Coordinate.description:
Coordinate is WGS84. `lng` rather than `lon`, matching H3, Valhalla and the
rest of this codebase — one spelling everywhere is worth more than any
argument about which.

clientSecret.description: Confirms this setup and nothing else, and is handed straight to Stripe.js.

idempotencyKey.description:
Generated client-side, so a retry over a flaky connection is recognised
rather than booked twice.

The generated TypeScript client sends it here, in the message. The gateway
also accepts an `Idempotency-Key` header and copies it into this field, for
callers that would rather describe the request than the trip — a proxy can
read a header without parsing a body. The handler prefers the field.
Generated client-side. The gateway also accepts an Idempotency-Key header.

v1EarningStatus.description:
- EARNING_STATUS_UNPAID: Owed, waiting for an account that can receive it.
 - EARNING_STATUS_REVERSED: Taken back after a refund or a dispute.

code.description:
A stable string a client may branch on. The set is the gRPC code names, so
it is closed and mechanical rather than invented per endpoint.

message.description:
For a human reading a log. Deliberately vague for anything internal — the
detail stays in the trace rather than travelling to a browser.

v1ErrorBody.description:
The one shape every failure takes on the REST edge.

Declared here rather than left to grpc-gateway's default because the gateway
does not use that default: `rest.go` installs a custom error handler, and for
as long as this message was absent the published document described a
`rpcStatus` — `{code: int, message, details}` — that nothing has ever
returned. A generated client believed it, and would have failed to decode
every error the server actually sends.

packageSlug.description:
Sedan, van and so on. A string rather than an enum because the catalogue is
operator configuration, not a protocol change.

surgeMultiplier.description:
The multiplier applied for demand in the pickup cell at quote time. Carried
explicitly so a rider can be shown why a fare is what it is.

saved.description:
False until the rider has saved a card. The card is then empty rather than
absent, like every unset field this API sends.

nextPageToken.description: Empty when there are no more.

owedCents.description: Earned and not yet sent to the driver's account, across all pages.

paidCents.description: Sent to the driver's account, across all pages.

nextPageToken.description: Empty when there are no more.

failureReason.description:
Why a failed payment failed: no_payment_method, declined,
authentication_failed or expired. Empty otherwise.

clientSecret.description:
Set while the status is REQUIRES_ACTION, for Stripe.js to run the rider's
authentication step, and only for the rider. Empty otherwise.

v1PaymentStatus.description: PaymentStatus is the payment state machine, as a client sees it.

requirementsDue.description:
The processor is waiting on the driver for something: send them back
through onboarding.

v1PayoutAccountStatus.description:
- PAYOUT_ACCOUNT_STATUS_NOT_STARTED: No account yet. Earnings are recorded and owed.
 - PAYOUT_ACCOUNT_STATUS_PENDING: An account that cannot receive money yet.
 - PAYOUT_ACCOUNT_STATUS_ACTIVE: Paid as trips complete.

v1PreviewTripRequest.description:
The caller is NOT a field on any request.

It arrives as gRPC metadata, put there by the gateway from a verified token.
This matters more now that the REST body maps straight onto the message: a
`rider_id` field would be client-supplied, and a client that can name the
rider can quote, book and read rides as somebody else.

fares.description: Quotes for each vehicle class, priced from the same route.

driverCents.description: The driver's part of it: their share of the fare, in proportion.

failureReason.description:
Why a failed refund failed, in the processor's words: a closed card, a
refusing bank.

v1RefundReversal.description:
RefundReversal is how a refund took the driver's share back.

 - REFUND_REVERSAL_NONE: Nothing was earned on the trip.
 - REFUND_REVERSAL_DEDUCTED: Not yet paid out: the driver is owed less.
 - REFUND_REVERSAL_REVERSED: Taken back from the driver's balance.
 - REFUND_REVERSAL_FAILED: The driver's balance could not cover it; the platform carries it.

v1RefundStatus.description:
RefundStatus is whether a refund reached the rider.

 - REFUND_STATUS_FAILED: It could not be delivered. The money is back with the platform, the
payment is refundable again, and the rider must be repaid another way.

polyline6.description:
Polyline encoded at precision 6, as Valhalla emits it. Not a repeated
Coordinate: a city route is hundreds of points, and the encoded form is
roughly a tenth the size on a connection a phone is paying for.

v1Route.description: Route is a driveable path with its cost.

running.description:
Running is how many driver goroutines are actually up, which lags
`drivers` for a moment after a rescale.

targetPingsPerSecond.description: Drivers divided by the interval: ingest's load, stated.

url.description:
Single use and short-lived: redirect to it at once, and never send it
anywhere else — it opens the driver's identity details to whoever follows
it.

driverId.description:
Empty until a driver is assigned, not absent: the gateway marshals with
EmitUnpopulated so a client can tell "unassigned" from "the server forgot".

v1TripStatus.description:
TripStatus is the state machine, and the wire is the place it is written
down once. UNSPECIFIED is reserved by convention so an unset field is not
silently a valid state.

 - TRIP_STATUS_UNMATCHED: No driver was found before the request expired. Distinct from cancelled:
nobody chose it, and the rider should be offered a retry rather than an
apology.
 - TRIP_STATUS_PAYMENT_PENDING: Waiting for the fare to be held on the rider's card. Nobody is dispatched to
a ride that cannot be paid for: payments answers within about a second, or
the trip is cancelled with the reason payment_failed. Numbered last rather
than first because enum numbers are the wire, and renumbering REQUESTED
would change what every stored and in-flight 1 means.

failureReason.description: Why a failed withdrawal failed, in the processor's words.
